scene.testo: Every ninety minutes, you would watch the sun rise over Earth. Sixteen sunrises in a single day. You would travel at 17,500 miles per hour, 250 miles up, inside a home that has no shower, no oven, and no down.

So how does anyone live like this? How do you wash, eat, sleep, and even use the bathroom when nothing stays where you put it? Every answer is stranger than you would guess, and some of them are a little gross.
But the real surprise is not the strange toilet or the missing shower. It is what the human body does after months without gravity, and what the crew must do every single day to stop it.

Let's start with the place itself. The International Space Station orbits about 250 miles above Earth. That is roughly the distance from New York City to Washington, D.C. and beyond, except straight up, in a vacuum.
The station is about 357 feet long from end to end. That is a little longer than an American football field, including both end zones. And it is flying over your head at 17,500 miles per hour.
Building it took years. The first piece, a Russian module named Zarya, launched in November 1998. The first crew moved in on November 2, 2000. Humans have lived aboard continuously ever since.
Before you can float in, you have to get there. Imagine you are strapped into a capsule on top of a rocket. The engines ignite. In about nine minutes, you go from standing still to orbital speed.

Two kinds of spacecraft carry crews to the station today. The Russian Soyuz has flown people for decades, and its design dates back to the 1960s. The SpaceX Crew Dragon is newer, with touchscreen controls inside.
Then comes docking. The capsule creeps toward the station and locks on to a port. Hooks latch. Pressure is checked again and again. Only after those checks do you open the hatch and float inside.

And now you are inside. Forget the open, carpeted decks from science fiction. The station is a set of connected tubes, called modules, joined together like a giant metal tinker toy floating above the planet.

Each module is a different room. Destiny is the main American science lab. Unity connects the American modules to the Russian side. Europe contributed the Columbus laboratory, and Japan built Kibo, its own large science lab.

NASA describes the pressurized living and working space as roughly the volume of a six-bedroom house. That sounds huge. But the walls, ceiling, and floor are all packed with equipment, cables, laptops, and storage lockers.
There is no wasted space up here. Every surface is a shelf, a desk, or a workstation. And since there is no gravity, you can use the ceiling and walls just as easily as the floor.

Moving around takes practice. On your first days, your brain gets confused. On Earth, the fluid in your inner ear tells you which way is down. In orbit, that signal disappears, and many astronauts feel dizzy and nauseous.

That feeling is called space adaptation syndrome, and it often fades within a few days. Handrails, labels, and lots of practice help. Soon you learn to push gently off a wall and glide exactly where you want to go.
Now, picture 6 AM. Your alarm goes off. You do not roll out of bed. You unzip a sleeping bag attached to the wall, and your arms drift up in front of you like you are underwater.

The station runs on Greenwich Mean Time, the same time zone as London. That way, mission control teams in the United States, Russia, Europe, and Japan can all agree on one schedule for the whole crew.
Here is a strange fact. The station circles Earth about every 90 minutes. That means you see roughly 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every 24 hours. Your body clock would be a mess without some help.

So the crew follows an Earth-style day. Lights inside the station can be adjusted to help signal morning and night. Sleep is scheduled for about eight hours, even when the windows show bright sunlight every forty-five minutes.
Now for the morning routine. There is no shower on the station. If you spray water in zero gravity, it does not fall. It clings to your skin and floats around as wobbling blobs.

So astronauts wash with rinseless soap and wet towels. They squeeze water from a pouch onto a cloth and wipe themselves clean. Hair gets washed with a rinseless shampoo, then towel dried. It works, but it is not a spa.

Brushing teeth is just as odd. You wet the brush, add toothpaste, and brush as usual. But you cannot spit into a sink the way you would at home. Many astronauts simply swallow the toothpaste, or spit it into a towel.

Clothes are another challenge. There is no washing machine on the station. Astronauts wear items for days, and exercise clothes get swapped out often. Used clothing is packed into cargo vehicles that burn up on reentry.

Then comes the question everyone asks. How do you use the toilet in zero gravity? The answer is airflow. A fan creates suction, pulling waste away from your body and into a container, instead of letting gravity do the job.

Now for the part that surprises everyone. Urine is not thrown away. A system collects it, along with moisture from the air, and processes it into clean drinking water. Yes, the crew drinks recycled water, including recycled sweat and urine.

NASA has said the water recovery system now recycles about 98 percent of the water on board. Every drop matters, because launching water from Earth is extremely expensive. Reusing it is how the station stays supplied.

That recycled water does more than quench thirst. Some of it is split by electricity into hydrogen and oxygen. The oxygen goes into the cabin air so you can breathe. The same water you drink also helps you inhale.

Meanwhile, carbon dioxide from your breath must be removed, or it builds up and makes you sick. Special scrubbers pull it from the air. Fans run constantly, because without gravity, your own breath can hang around your face.

Now it is time for breakfast. Most station food is packaged in pouches and containers. Many meals are dried, so astronauts add water using a special dispenser, then wait a few minutes for the food to rehydrate.

Other foods come ready to eat. There are thermostabilized pouches, canned items, snacks, and drinks in sealed bags. Astronauts warm meals in a small food warmer, then use scissors to open the package and a spoon to eat.

Crumbs are a real problem. A floating crumb can drift into your eyes, or get sucked into an air vent and damage equipment. That is why astronauts often choose tortillas over bread. Tortillas make far fewer crumbs.

Salt and pepper come as liquids. Dry salt and pepper would float everywhere, and could be inhaled or clog the filters. So the crew uses liquid versions, squeezed out of small containers. Even seasoning needs a space-age solution.

Fresh food is a treat. When a cargo ship arrives, it sometimes carries fruit, such as apples or oranges. Astronauts have said these fresh items are special, because most of their diet is packaged and processed.

Now comes the hardest part of the day. Exercise. Astronauts work out about two hours every day. Without that routine, muscles shrink and bones weaken, because the body no longer fights gravity all day long.
There is a treadmill, a stationary bike, and a resistance machine. You must be strapped down, or you would float away mid-run. Bungee cords pull you toward the belt, giving you a feeling of weight.

The resistance machine uses vacuum cylinders to simulate lifting weights. Astronauts can do squats, deadlifts, and presses. NASA says that without exercise, astronauts can lose bone density at a rate of about one percent per month.

Even with all that work, the body changes. Fluids shift toward the head, so faces look puffy and noses feel stuffy. Legs can look thinner. And some astronauts experience changes in their eyesight during long missions.

When astronauts return home, many feel heavy and weak. Standing up can make them dizzy, because their bodies forgot how to handle gravity. Recovery takes weeks, and teams help them rebuild strength through careful exercise programs.

But astronauts do not just exercise and eat. They are working scientists. Most of the day is filled with experiments on biology, physics, medicine, and materials, all studied in the unique environment of microgravity.

Some experiments grow plants. Astronauts have grown lettuce, radishes, and other crops in orbit. NASA says the crew first ate lettuce grown on the station in August 2015. Growing food will matter on future long missions.

Other jobs are simple maintenance. Astronauts fix pumps, replace filters, clean vents, and update equipment. The station is a machine that must be kept alive, and the crew are its mechanics, plumbers, and electricians.

Sometimes the job requires going outside. A spacewalk is a major event. Astronauts spend hours preparing, and the walk itself often lasts six or seven hours, in a suit that is basically a personal spacecraft.

Out there, the temperature swings are brutal. NASA says sunlit surfaces can reach about 250 degrees Fahrenheit, while shaded areas can fall to about minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit. The suit must protect you from both extremes.
Back inside, your day ends with time to call home. Astronauts can email, make video calls, and talk to family. Seeing Earth through the window is a daily reminder of how far from home you really are.
Then it is bedtime. Your bed is a sleeping bag tied to the wall of a small crew cabin, about the size of a phone booth. You zip in, and your arms float freely in front of you.
There is no up, so there is no pillow in the usual sense. Many astronauts say they sleep well anyway. Some wear eye masks and earplugs, because the station hums with fans and pumps all night long.

So here is the most surprising detail. Everything you do on Earth without thinking, washing, eating, sleeping, even breathing, becomes a designed system in orbit. Nothing is automatic. Every day is engineered, so humans can live 250 miles above home.

descrizione:
What is life really like inside the International Space Station? In this Orbital Days documentary, we follow a full day aboard the ISS, 250 miles above Earth, traveling at 17,500 miles per hour. Discover how astronauts wash, eat, sleep, exercise, and use the toilet in zero gravity.

You will learn how the station recycles water, how astronauts handle space food, why exercise is required for two hours every day, and what spacewalks are like. All facts come from NASA and astronaut accounts, with US units throughout.

If you love space exploration, astronaut life, and the science of living in microgravity, subscribe to Orbital Days for more journeys beyond our atmosphere.
